Q: Ctrl + Space Not Working Properly Android Studio A:

2026

I ran into some issues with autocomplete not working how I'd expect in Android Studio and everything was fixed with this change:

Settings > Editor > General > Code Completion > Machine Learning-Assisted Completion

Turn that off and everything starts working again.

Q: Why does JSON not allow encoding infinities and NaN? A:

Douglas Crockford’s talk “JSON: The Fat-Free Alternative to XML”, as transcribed on JSON.org, gives this explanation:

A number can be represented as integer, real, or floating point. JSON does not support octal or hex because it is minimal. It does not have values for NaN or Infinity because it does not want to be tied to any particular internal representation.

This is a somewhat cryptic explanation. But I think an excerpt from another one of his talks, “The JSON Saga” can help interpret it:

JSON is the intersection […] of all modern programming languages. All languages have some sense of data, and structures of data. […] Every language expresses these differently, and will add a lot of other stuff on top of it, like type systems, and semantics. But they all have the same idea about what the data looks like, and JSON has the thing that's common to everything. By being at the intersection, it turns out to be the thing that everybody can agree on, so it's really easy to pass data back and forth. Prior data interchange formats tended to try to be the union of all the languages, and that turns out to be horrendously complex, and really difficult to deal with. JSON, by being so simple, actually became really easy to use.

So the desire was to only provide common, timeless data types and structures. And it seems like infinities and NaNs were deemed not timeless enough, too likely to cause interoperability problems, too much attached to the particulars of IEEE 754 to be worth including.

Ironically, most (schema-less) implementations of JSON do parse numbers into IEEE 754 doubles anyway, which enables representing infinity in JSON as, for example, 9e999, by counting on the recipient to round that to infinity upon parsing. But that’s likely to cause interoperability problems with implementations that, for once, do try to parse numbers of arbitrary precision losslessly; thus creating the very kind of encroachment of implementation details that Crockford seems to have wanted to avoid. If infinities were representable in JSON directly, this interoperability problem would not exist. (I could, however, defend omitting NaNs – null should probably suffice for the purpose of representing absent or invalid values.)

Q: C, structs and pointers - why does this work? A:

Now that I think about it - maybe best practice would be to do some magic number like:

memset(&c, 0xCC, sizeof c);

I often leave objects uninitialized so that potentially it crashes when something like this happens but as others have pointed out this is not guaranteed.

And not '0x0' because often that is intended as a possible value.

And also, there are tagged pointers on the topic (on some modern architectures where it's supported).

Q: Problem Flet Python code : expand option not working A:

I made own minimal working example and tested it with bgcolor= to see which object has problem with expanding.

Problem makes Column which doesn't use full width even with expand=True.

It needs also horizontal_alignment=ft.CrossAxisAlignment.STRETCH,

content=ft.Column(
    [
         # ... cards ...
    ],
    spacing=10,
    expand=True,
    horizontal_alignment=ft.CrossAxisAlignment.STRETCH,
),

Full working code:

import flet as ft


def main(page: ft.Page):
    page.title = "Flet Layout Example"

    # Minimal placeholder for IPBox (list of controls)
    IPBox = [
        ft.TextField(label="IP 1"),
        ft.TextField(label="IP 2"),
        ft.TextField(label="IP 3"),
    ]

    mainpage = ft.Row(
        controls=[
            ft.Container(
                content=ft.Card(
                    content=ft.Container(
                        content=ft.Column(
                            [
                                ft.Text(
                                    "Select your IP",
                                    weight=ft.FontWeight.BOLD,
                                    size=18,
                                    text_align=ft.TextAlign.CENTER,
                                ),
                                *IPBox,
                            ],
                            spacing=5,
                            horizontal_alignment=ft.CrossAxisAlignment.CENTER,
                        ),
                        padding=20,
                    )
                ),
                expand=True,
            ),
            ft.Container(
                content=ft.Column(
                    [
                        ft.Container(
                            content=ft.Card(
                                content=ft.Container(
                                    content=ft.Text("Card 1"),
                                    padding=20,
                                ),
                                expand=1,
                            ),
                            expand=True,
                            # bgcolor="green",
                        ),
                        ft.Container(
                            content=ft.Card(
                                content=ft.Container(
                                    content=ft.Text("Card 1"),
                                    padding=20,
                                ),
                                expand=1,
                            ),
                            expand=True,
                            # bgcolor="green",
                        ),
                        ft.Container(
                            content=ft.Card(
                                content=ft.Container(
                                    content=ft.Text("Card 1"),
                                    padding=20,
                                ),
                                expand=1,
                            ),
                            expand=True,
                            # bgcolor="green",
                        ),
                    ],
                    spacing=10,
                    expand=True,
                    horizontal_alignment=ft.CrossAxisAlignment.STRETCH,
                ),
                expand=True,
                # bgcolor="red",
            ),
        ],
        expand=True,
    )

    page.add(mainpage)


ft.app(target=main)

Q: Why is iframe a pair tag A:

Now in HTML5, per MDN and the W3 spec, the children of iframe elements no longer have any meaning at all:

https://dev.w3.org/html5/spec-LC/the-iframe-element.html#the-iframe-element

"Descendants of iframe elements represent nothing. (In legacy user agents that do not support iframe elements, the contents would be parsed as markup that could act as fallback content.)"

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/iframe

"Permitted content: None."
